decisions.quote:
A recent study by Riccucci et al. (2016) indicates that symbolic gender representation is an important quality for
citizen–state interactions. Increasing the representation of female officials positively affected the willingness to
co-produce in a recycling initiative. The results suggest that women were more willing to co-produce when encountering higher shares of female officials. These findings promise considerable benefits for public organizations, as
symbolic representation may lead to better services as well as cost savings (Riccucci & Van Ryzin, 2017). However,
Van Ryzin et al. (2017) conducted a recent replication with a different policy context that could not confirm the
findings. Symbolic representation did not unfold in the context of emergency preparation.
Consequently, Van Ryzin et al. (2017) proposed additional replication studies “as an opportunity to further
develop and test the underlying theory of symbolic representation to more deeply probe its mechanisms and contingencies” (p. 1376). Following this notion, the present study provides a wide replication (Walker et al., 2019) of the
original research by Riccucci et al. (2016).
decisions.reason: Row 540 lists Riccucci & Van Ryzin (2017, Public Administration Review 77(1), 21-30, DOI: 10.1111/puar.12649, 'Representative bureaucracy: a lever to enhance social equity, coproduction, and democracy'). In the primary text, that article is cited solely as theoretical and conceptual background on symbolic representation (lines 72-73, 78-79, 109-117, 130-132, 1223-1225). The sole empirical study re-tested by Sievert (2021) is Riccucci, Van Ryzin, & Li (2016, DOI: 10.1111/puar.12401), which is already present in shipped row 541 (paired with blind target 0), while Van Ryzin et al. (2017) is discussed as an earlier replication. Because 10.1111/puar.12649 is a background-only citation with no replacement target left unrepresented, row 540 should be removed.

decisions.quote: The replication's results do not confirm the findings outlined by Riccucci et al. (2016). In the present study, symbolic gender representation does not affect the willingness to co-produce. Equivalence testing (Lakens, 2017) indicates null findings based on the absence of meaningful treatment effects.
decisions.reason: Outcomes are original-specific. Because row 540's shipped original (Riccucci & Van Ryzin, 2017, DOI: 10.1111/puar.12649) is a conceptual background reference rather than a tested target (resolved to remove_row on original), the paper neither re-tests nor reports a replication outcome for it; the paper's failed replication verdict applies exclusively to Riccucci, Van Ryzin, & Li (2016, DOI: 10.1111/puar.12401) in row 541.

decisions.quote:
Following this notion, the present study provides a wide replication (Walker et al., 2019) of the
original research by Riccucci et al. (2016). The preregistered survey experiment is set in the policy field of criminal
justice, a context that features the co-production of areas such as prisoner rehabilitation (Loeffler & Bovaird, 2020).
Applying the judicial system allows adding meaningful contextual variation to the design (Tsang & Kwan, 1999) by
testing the effects of symbolic representation in a context with greater organizational integration of the coproduction efforts (Nabatchi et al., 2017). This replication provides new data from a sample of 1000 citizens and
allows extending the original analytical strategy with robustness tests, such as a manipulation check.
decisions.reason: Both shipped and blind coding agree that the FLoRA record (Sievert, 2021, DOI: 10.1111/padm.12743) is a replication study collecting new survey-experiment data from 1,000 German citizens to re-test Riccucci et al. (2016) (captured in row 541, whereas row 540's background citation is removed via the original field).
